Let \(A_r\) be the \(20\times20\) adjacency matrix for pairs of triples at Johnson distance \(r\). Then
\[
D_p=(d(A,B)^p)_{A,B}=A_1+2^pA_2+3^pA_3.
\]
The Johnson scheme \(J(6,3)\) has four common eigenspaces of dimensions
\[
1,\ 5,\ 9,\ 5.
\]
On the three nonconstant eigenspaces the eigenvalues of \(A_1,A_2,A_3\) are
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccc}
& A_1&A_2&A_3\\ \hline
V_1&3&-3&-1\\
V_2&-1&-1&1\\
V_3&-3&3&-1
\end{array}
\]
so the eigenvalues of \(D_p\) on the zero-sum subspace are
\[
\theta_1=3-3\cdot2^p-3^p,\qquad
\theta_2=-1-2^p+3^p,\qquad
\theta_3=-3+3\cdot2^p-3^p.
\]
For \(0<p\le1\), concavity gives \(3^p\le2^p+1\), hence \(\theta_2\le0\). Also
\[
g(p)=3^p-3\cdot2^p+3
\]
is decreasing on \([0,1]\), since \(g'(p)=3^p\log3-3\cdot2^p\log2<0\) there, and \(g(1)=0\), so \(\theta_3\le0\). Finally \(\theta_1<0\). For \(p>1\), \(3^p>2^p+1\), so \(\theta_2>0\). Thus
\[
\wp=1.
\]

At \(p=1\), the kernel on the zero-sum subspace is
\[
E=V_2\oplus V_3,
\]
so
\[
\dim E=9+5=14.
\]
Equivalently, for \(c=(c_A)\),
\[
\sum_{A,B}c_Ac_Bd(A,B)
=-\sum_{i=1}^6\left(\sum_{A\ni i}c_A\right)^2,
\]
so
\[
E=\left\{c:\sum_{A\ni i}c_A=0\text{ for every }i\in[6]\right\}.
\]

Now let \(S\subseteq X\). A subspace of \(E\) supported in \(S\) has dimension
\[
|S|-\operatorname{rank} M_S,
\]
where \(M_S\) is the \(6\times |S|\) incidence matrix of the triples in \(S\). Hence a four-dimensional subspace supported in \(S\) requires
\[
|S|-\operatorname{rank}M_S\ge4.
\]

The minimum is \(8\). Indeed, if \([6]\) is partitioned into three pairs, say
\[
\{1,2\}\sqcup\{3,4\}\sqcup\{5,6\},
\]
then the eight triples choosing one element from each pair have incidence rank \(4\), so their kernel has dimension \(8-4=4\). Conversely, any \(S\) with \(|S|\le7\) has \(\operatorname{rank}M_S\ge |S|-3\), so the kernel dimension is at most \(3\). Equality for \(|S|=8\) occurs exactly for these “one from each pair” supports. Therefore
\[
d_4=8.
\]

There are
\[
\frac{6!}{2^3\,3!}=15
\]
partitions of \([6]\) into three unordered pairs, and each gives one extremal four-dimensional subspace. Hence
\[
N_4=15.
\]

So \(\mathcal M\) is naturally the set of perfect matchings of \(K_6\). Two extremal subspaces intersect nontrivially exactly when the corresponding pair partitions share one pair. Thus \(\Gamma\) is the graph on perfect matchings of \(K_6\), adjacent when they share an edge.

For a fixed matching, choose the shared edge in \(3\) ways; on the remaining four vertices there are \(2\) matchings different from the original. Thus
\[
k=3\cdot2=6.
\]
If two matchings are adjacent, they share one edge; the only third matching adjacent to both and containing that shared edge is obtained by using the third matching on the remaining four vertices, so
\[
\lambda=1.
\]
If two matchings are nonadjacent, their union is a \(6\)-cycle, and exactly the three alternate perfect matchings of that cycle meet both, so
\[
\mu=3.
\]
Thus \(\Gamma\) is strongly regular with parameters \((15,6,1,3)\).

\[
\boxed{(\wp,\dim E,d_4,N_4,k,\lambda,\mu)=(1,14,8,15,6,1,3)}.
\]
